attributes.nuance_translation: An expression used to show a relatively high level of skill in something.

attributes.body:
～のが上手（じょうず） is a phrase that behaves in almost exactly the same way as ～のが好（す）き, but rather than meaning 'to like' something, it means 'to be good at' something. This particular expression is used with the plain (dictionary) form of verbs only.

In these examples, we can see that there is no difference between Ichidan verbs and Godan verbs. Both will appear in their plain form. In this expression, のが is performing the same function as in the regular のは・のが construction. This function is nominalization (turning a phrase into a noun).

Caution

If you want to express that you were good at something (in the past), the verb will still remain in the plain form, but 上手（じょうず） will change to the past tense.

Caution

This grammar point can sound a little bit arrogant if you are referring to your own skills, so the word 得意（とくい） may also be used if you want to sound a bit more humble.

These two opposite terms are used after verbs to express being good or bad at certain actions. のが上手 is used to say someone is good at something, as in 絵を描くのが上手 ('She is good at drawing'). In contrast, 絵を描くのが下手 means 'She is not good at drawing.' Note that in Japanese culture, it's uncommon to use 上手 to describe yourself, as it can come across as boastful.

second_relatable.title: のがへた
second_relatable.meaning: To be bad at, Poor at, Unskillful

attributes.body: These phrases combine the nominalizer, or 'dummy noun,' の with the な-Adjectives 好き and 上手. They are used to express liking something (好き) or being good at something (上手) by attaching them to a verb. In Japanese culture, boasting about one's abilities is rare, so 絵を描くのが好き might be preferred over 上手 when talking about being good at drawing.
